procedural_history.impugned_order: Orders of the High Court of Judicature at Madras dated 24th October, 1945, in A.A.O. Nos. 372 of 1943 and 634 of 1944 which were appeals from the orders of the Subordinate Judge of Ellore in E.A. No. 440 of 1937 and C.M.P. No. 152 of 1943 in O.S. No. 87 of 1923.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The judgment-debtors filed two petitions: a review petition to the High Court and a petition to the trial Court. The trial Court dismissed the latter petition. The judgment-debtors appealed this dismissal. The High Court heard the appeal and the review petition together. The High Court directed the decree-holder's counsel to elect whether his client would deposit the purchase money into Court or have the sale set aside. The decree-holder elected to retain the property and pay the purchase money. The High Court held that the mortgagor's village had been sold, he did not come within the purview of cl. (D) of the proviso to s- 3 of the Madras Agriculturists' Relief Act and so he was entitled to claim relief under t.be Act and the debt stcod discharged under the provision of the Act, but the sale was not liable to be set aside ; and in accordrtnce with this judgment the decree-bolder wa• directed to pay the amount !o1· wbicb the property had been sold with interest thereon.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant (decree-holder) obtained leave to appeal from the High Court and preferred appeals to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court reversed the judgment of the Madras High Court.

issue.issue_text: When an appeal is preferred from an order rejecting an application under Order XXI, Rule 90 of the Code of Civil Procedure to set aside an execution sale, whether the sale becomes absolute before the matter is finally decided by the appellate court.

facts: An application was made under Order XXI, Rule 90 of the Code of Civil Procedure to set aside a sale in execution.
The Subordinate Judge disallowed this application and confirmed the sale.
An appeal was then filed against the Subordinate Judge's decision to not set aside the sale.
law: Under the Code of Civil Procedure, an appellate court (like the High Court) has the same powers as the original trial court (the Subordinate Judge).

The court cited a Privy Council decision which held that for the purpose of the Limitation Act, the 'time when the sale becomes absolute' is when the High Court disposes of the appeal, not when the original court confirms it.
application: The court reasoned that as long as an appeal is pending, there is no finality to the lower court's order confirming the sale.
The order of the trial court confirming the sale only becomes truly final and absolute when the appeal against the refusal to set it aside is dismissed by the appellate court.
The court stated that the true position is that there is no finality until the litigation is finally determined by the appellate court.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that when an appeal is preferred from an order rejecting an application to set aside an execution sale, the sale does not become absolute until the matter is finally decided by the appellate court.

issue.issue_text: Whether the judgment-debtors were entitled to relief under the Madras Agriculturists' Relief Act on the ground that they ceased to be owners of the property from the date of the court sale, even while their appeal to set aside that sale was pending.

facts: A village owned by the judgment-debtors was sold in a court-ordered execution sale.
The judgment-debtors filed an application to set aside the sale, which was dismissed, and the sale was confirmed.
The judgment-debtors then appealed the order that refused to set aside the sale.
While this appeal was pending, they also applied for relief under the Madras Agriculturists' Relief Act, arguing they were eligible because the sale meant they were no longer owners of the village.
law: The key legal principle applied by the court is that when an appeal is filed against an order refusing to set aside an execution sale, the sale does not become absolute until the appeal is finally decided by the appellate court.
application: The Supreme Court found the High Court's reasoning to be self-contradictory, noting that if the sale was effective, the debt was satisfied, and there would be no basis to invoke the Act.
The Court's primary reasoning was that the High Court was wrong to assume the judgment-debtors had ceased to be owners from the date of the sale.
Because the judgment-debtors' appeal to set aside the sale was still pending, the sale had not yet become absolute.
As the sale was not yet absolute, legal ownership had not passed, and the judgment-debtors were still considered the owners of the village.
As owners, they were disqualified from relief by clause (D) of the proviso to section 3 of the Madras Agriculturists' Relief Act.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the judgment-debtors' claim for relief, holding that they did not cease to be owners of the property while their appeal to set aside the sale was pending. Because the sale had not become absolute, they remained the legal owners and were therefore disqualified from receiving relief under the Act.

issue.issue_text: Whether the application for leave to appeal was barred by limitation, thereby making the present appeals not maintainable.

facts: The respondents raised a preliminary objection that the appellant's application for leave to appeal was barred by limitation.
The appellant had filed an affidavit in the High Court explaining that the delay was mainly caused by the proceedings for the review of the High Court's order.
The High Court accepted this explanation and exercised its discretion to condone the delay.
law: Section 5 of the Limitation Act allows a court to excuse a delay if the applicant provides a 'sufficient reason'.
application: The Supreme Court noted that the High Court had already considered the reasons for the delay and found them to be sufficient.
The Supreme Court determined that it could not override the discretion that had been exercised by the High Court in this matter.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the issue of delay could not be reopened in the present appeals. Consequently, the objection was rejected, and the appeals were found to be maintainable.

issue.issue_text: Whether the appellant was estopped from pursuing the appeals after his counsel had elected in the High Court to retain the property and pay the purchase money.

facts: The High Court gave the appellant (decree-holder) a choice to either deposit the purchase money and retain the property he had purchased, or have the sale set aside.
On November 15, 1946, the appellant's counsel informed the High Court that his client elected to retain the property and pay the purchase money.
law: For a party to be estopped from appealing an order by reason of an election made pursuant to that order, there must be evidence on the record showing that the party consented to be bound by the order and waived their right to appeal.
application: The respondents argued that because the appellant's counsel had stated his client's choice to retain the property and pay the money, the appellant was now estopped from appealing the High Court's order.
The Supreme Court found this objection to be "entirely devoid of any substance."

The Court reasoned that there was nothing on the record to prove that the appellant, by making the election, had consented to be bound by the High Court's order or had waived his right to appeal against it.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the estoppel argument, holding that the appellant's election in the High Court did not prevent him from pursuing the appeals, as there was no evidence he had waived his right to do so.

issue.issue_text: Whether the respondents could challenge the validity of the sale in these appeals when they had not filed an appeal against the High Court's order upholding the sale.

facts: The respondents contended that the sale of the property should have been set aside due to a material irregularity.
The specific irregularity alleged was that the permission given to the decree-holder to bid and set off the price was for an earlier sale, not the one that ultimately took place.
This same argument had been presented to the lower courts (the Subordinate Judge and the High Court) and was rejected by both.
The High Court, in its order, had explicitly upheld the validity of the sale.
law: A party cannot challenge a part of a lower court's decision in an appeal unless they have filed their own appeal against that specific part of the order.
application: The Court observed that while the respondents were challenging the validity of the sale in the current proceedings, they had not filed their own appeal against the High Court's order which had explicitly upheld that same sale.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the respondents' challenge, concluding that they could not raise the issue of the sale's validity in these appeals because they had failed to file their own appeal against the High Court's order that upheld the sale.

arguments.issue_text: When an appeal is preferred from an order rejecting an application under Order XXI, Rule 90 of the Code of Civil Procedure to set aside an execution sale, whether the sale becomes absolute before the matter is finally decided by the appellate court.
appellant_arguments: The sale and the satisfaction of the decree are not final while an appeal to set aside the sale is pending. The same approach should be applied to both the sale and the satisfaction of the decree; if one is not final, the other cannot be considered final either.
respondent_arguments: The sale becomes absolute on the date it occurs, regardless of a pending appeal. This is evidenced by the High Court's finding that the judgment-debtors ceased to be owners of the property from the date of the sale.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the judgment-debtors were entitled to relief under the Madras Agriculturists' Relief Act on the ground that they ceased to be owners of the property from the date of the court sale, even while their appeal to set aside that sale was pending.
appellant_arguments: The judgment-debtors cannot take an inconsistent position. They cannot claim the sale was final for the purpose of qualifying as agriculturists under the Act, while simultaneously appealing to have that same sale set aside. If the sale was not final due to the pending appeal, they had not ceased to be owners and were therefore not entitled to relief under the Act.
respondent_arguments: They were entitled to relief because the court sale made them cease to be owners of the property, which in turn qualified them as agriculturists under the Act, leading to the discharge of their debt.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the application for leave to appeal was barred by limitation, thereby making the present appeals not maintainable.
appellant_arguments: The delay in filing the application was caused by the review proceedings in the High Court, which constituted sufficient reason for the delay. The High Court exercised its discretion to condone the delay, and this decision should not be overturned.
respondent_arguments: The application for leave to appeal was filed after the limitation period had expired. The reasons provided for the delay did not constitute 'sufficient reason' under section 5 of the Limitation Act, and therefore the appeals were not maintainable.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the appellant was estopped from pursuing the appeals after his counsel had elected in the High Court to retain the property and pay the purchase money.
appellant_arguments: The election made by counsel in the High Court did not constitute a waiver of the right to appeal. There is no evidence on record to show that the appellant consented to be bound by the High Court's order and gave up his right to appeal.
respondent_arguments: The appellant was estopped from appealing because his counsel had made a clear election in the High Court to retain the property and pay the purchase money. This action amounted to an acceptance of the High Court's order, barring any subsequent appeal.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the respondents could challenge the validity of the sale in these appeals when they had not filed an appeal against the High Court's order upholding the sale.
appellant_arguments: The respondents were precluded from challenging the validity of the sale in these appeals. The High Court had already ruled against them on this point, and by not filing their own appeal against that part of the order, they had accepted the finding that the sale was valid.
respondent_arguments: The sale was invalid and should have been set aside by the High Court.

cases.principle: When an appeal is filed against an order refusing to set aside an execution sale (under Order XXI, rule 90), the sale does not become absolute until the appeal is finally decided by the appellate court. Therefore, the limitation period under Article 180 of the Indian Limitation Act for the purchaser to apply for delivery of possession runs from the date of the appellate court's order, not the date of the original court's order confirming the sale.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When an appeal is filed against an order related to an execution sale, such as an order refusing to set it aside, there is no finality to the sale or related orders, like the recording of the decree's satisfaction, until the litigation is finally determined by the appellate court.
obiter: Where immovable property is sold in execution of a decree and the sale has become absolute, the property is deemed to have vested in the purchaser from the time the property is sold, not from the time the sale becomes absolute.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The High Court's judgment was self-contradictory and could not be sustained. It was inconsistent to hold that the judgment-debtors had ceased to be owners of the property from the date of the execution sale (thereby qualifying for relief under the Madras Act), while simultaneously upholding the validity of that same sale. The correct legal position is that when an appeal against an order refusing to set aside a sale is pending, there is no finality to the sale or the satisfaction of the decree until the appeal is finally determined. Consequently, the judgment-debtors had not ceased to be owners and were not entitled to relief under the Act.
legal_tests_applied: When an appeal is preferred from an order refusing to set aside a sale under Order XXI, rule 90, there is no finality to the sale until the litigation is finally determined by the appellate Court.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant did not lose; the appeals were allowed. The respondent's arguments failed for the following reasons:

The respondents' core argument was based on a logical inconsistency. They could not claim the sale was final for the purpose of qualifying as agriculturists under the Madras Act, while simultaneously challenging the finality of that same sale through an appeal.
The respondents were precluded from challenging the validity of the sale in these appeals because they had not filed their own appeal against the part of the High Court's order that upheld the sale.
The respondents' preliminary objection that the appeal was barred by limitation was rejected, as the Court refused to override the discretion exercised by the High Court in condoning the delay.

The respondents' preliminary objection that the appellant was estopped from appealing was rejected because there was no evidence on record to show that the appellant had waived his right to appeal by electing to retain the property in the High Court.
why_respondent_won: The respondent did not win; the appeals were allowed. The appellant's arguments succeeded for the following reasons:

The Court accepted the appellant's primary contention that the High Court's position was self-contradictory. If the sale was effective, the decree was satisfied, and the Madras Act could not be invoked. If the Act applied and discharged the debt, the sale itself could not stand.

The Court adopted the appellant's reasoning that the finality of the sale and the finality of the order recording satisfaction of the decree must be treated consistently. As an appeal regarding the sale was pending, neither could be considered final.
The Court agreed that because the sale was not final, the judgment-debtors had not ceased to be owners of the property and were therefore not entitled to relief under the Madras Act.
policy_considerations: A party cannot maintain an inconsistent legal position. The finality of an execution sale and the finality of the satisfaction of the decree resulting from that sale must be treated consistently. As the court stated, 'The sale and satisfaction must go together and if finality is to be attached to the sale it should have been held to attach also to the order recording satisfaction of the decree.'
